2023A-p1#c: Start by writing two rows: input in the language, input outside it. Put the acceptance bounds for each class in those rows. Do not start with a majority vote: both original bounds are below one half.

For the amplification direction, count accepting runs and compare their fraction with the midpoint of one eighth and one quarter. The distance from either promised rate to this midpoint is one sixteenth. Choose enough independent trials for the tail probability to be at most the target error.
Have you proved both inclusions, analysed both input cases, and kept polynomial runtime? For the easy inclusion, finitely many short input lengths may need to be hardcoded.
2024C-p1#c: Write the two acceptance conditions when both thresholds equal one half. Ask whether an algorithm that ignores the input could satisfy both.

Test the algorithm ‘flip a fair coin and accept on heads’. Then ask whether a genuine positive-gap, polynomial-time randomized decider could decide an undecidable language: enumerate its finitely many random-bit strings.

To disprove equality, explain both why the no-gap class contains every language and why the positive-gap class contains only decidable languages. Merely saying ‘there is no gap’ is not a complete proof.
hw2026s3-p3#d: Write one indicator for a vertex surviving the threshold. The same random threshold is used for all vertices; do not invent separate independent thresholds.

For a fixed vertex, its survival event is that the uniform threshold lies between zero and its fractional vertex weight. Check that this weight lies in the unit interval, then use the length of that interval.
Did you define the indicator, justify the weight range and use linearity without claiming independence? The conclusion concerns the expected number of vertices, not a density ratio.
hw2026s3-p3#e: Repeat part (d)'s setup for edges, using the edge weight rather than a product of endpoint weights. Read the definition of the edge threshold set carefully.

An edge survives exactly when the common threshold is at most its fractional edge weight. Use feasibility to put that weight in the unit interval, compute its survival probability, and sum over edges.
Does your event use the edge weight from the LP? Multiplying endpoint probabilities would incorrectly assume independent endpoint thresholds.
hw2026s2-p2#a: First check the random-graph convention. For a uniformly random simple loopless regular graph, a fixed vertex has only the other vertices as possible neighbours; diagonal pairs are not exchangeable with off-diagonal pairs.

Define one edge indicator per ordered pair. In the simple loopless model symmetry gives probability \(d/(n-1)\) for distinct endpoints, so the expectation is \(d(|S||T|-|S\cap T|)/(n-1)\). The supplied solution instead uses all pairs with denominator \(n\); that needs a different model and does not follow from relabeling symmetry alone.

This source has a convention issue, not a missing trick. State the assumed graph model and do not claim diagonal and off-diagonal pairs have identical probabilities. The later mixing-lemma main term is not automatically an exact random-graph expectation.
hw2025s1-p1#a: Make two headings: turn expected time into a timeout; turn ‘don't know’ into retries. These are two separate algorithms.

In the first direction, stop after a constant multiple of the expected polynomial bound and return ‘don't know’ on timeout. In the other, rerun independently until a committed answer appears; its constant success probability bounds the expected number of attempts.
Did you prove committed answers are always correct? Distinguish worst-case polynomial time for the timeout algorithm from expected polynomial time for repeated trials.
hw2025s1-p1#b: Write RP's acceptance guarantees separately for yes- and no-inputs. Identify which one needs improvement to meet the BPP definition.
Try two independent runs and accept if either accepts. Calculate the probability both reject on a yes-input. For coRP, reverse the roles: reject if either run rejects.
Have you specified OR versus AND correctly, preserved the error-free side, and checked both BPP thresholds? Repetition without an output rule is incomplete.
hw2025s1-p1#c: Use part (a)'s bounded-time ‘don't know’ characterization. For one inclusion, decide how to replace ‘don't know’; for the reverse, identify which outputs of RP and coRP are certain to be correct.

Replacing ‘don't know’ by reject yields an RP candidate, and replacing it by accept yields a coRP candidate. In the reverse direction, trust an RP acceptance or a coRP rejection; otherwise abstain. Amplify their uncertain sides first if necessary.
Check each input case: the two trusted outputs cannot contradict one another. Bound abstention and runtime, and explicitly conclude both inclusions.
2017A-p1#a: Write the three recursive calls and combine the split and combine costs into one local-work term. A bounded-size base case is constant asymptotically.

Compare the total child work with the parent work. Three children each have one quarter of the input size, so linear local work decreases by a factor of three quarters per level. Alternatively compare the master-theorem exponent with one.
Have you included all recursive calls, summed level work, bounded leaves and used the root for a matching lower bound? Do not multiply every level by the root's cost.
2017A-p1#b: Write the first three local costs while halving both matrix dimensions. There is one recursive call, not one per row or column.
Factor out the initial sum of dimensions. The remaining level factors form a geometric series with ratio one half. Include the terminal row's work using its reduced width.
Does your bound include the base-case row and a root-level lower bound? The recursion depth alone does not determine the total cost.
2017A-p1#c: Identify the two scalar coefficients in the expression. Is the operation a sum, a product, or something nonlinear?
Apply linearity with coefficients two and minus one. If the dependence distracts you, expand expectation as a weighted sum over outcomes and distribute the sum.
Mention that independence is unnecessary for finite expectations. Do not justify this using the product rule for independent variables.
2018A-p1#b: Write the recurrence from the two unequal child sizes and the dominant local work. The usual equal-size master theorem does not directly fit.
Square each child-size fraction and add them to obtain the ratio of child-level quadratic work to parent work. This ratio is strictly less than one, so use a geometric upper bound.
Did you square the fractions because local work is quadratic, account for leaves, and provide the root's matching lower bound?
2018B-p4#a: Imagine the input array is fixed adversarially before any pivot is chosen. Is there still randomness left in the execution?

Check whether the selection analysis assumes a distribution on input arrays or only a uniform pivot among the current elements. This determines whether its expected bound applies to every fixed input.
Do not confuse worst-case input with worst-case random choices. State explicitly what the expectation averages over.
2018B-p4#b: Name the random experiment that produces two potentially different runtimes on the same fixed input.
Describe the sequence of random pivot choices made during the run. Their ranks determine subsequent subproblem sizes; the input is held fixed while taking the expectation.
Do not average uniformly over all possible full pivot sequences: they need not have equal probabilities because their conditional subproblem sizes differ.
2018B-p4#c: For pivot rank \(j\), write the two side sizes \(j-1\) and \(n-j\). Selection pays for at most one side after partitioning.

Use a nondecreasing worst-case expected-cost bound for the larger possible side, then average over pivot ranks. For even input size, each upper-half side size occurs twice. Handle rounding as permitted by the question.
Explain the factor two and the summation limits. Do not sum both recursive sides as quicksort would, or silently assume a size-dependent runtime is monotone without using a monotone upper bound.
2018B-p4#d: Write the target as an explicit upper bound with an unknown constant, and replace the partition-cost term by a second constant times input size.

Substitute the linear inductive hypothesis into the upper-half sum. For even input size, the sum of its indices is at most three eighths of the square of the input size. The recursive contribution then uses at most three quarters of the desired linear bound.
Choose the induction constant at least four times the partition-cost constant and large enough for base cases. Use inequalities rather than an approximate arithmetic-series calculation in the proof.
2024B-p3#x: Let the number of distinct minimum cuts be an unknown integer. Fix one of those cuts before running contraction; do not merely use the probability of finding some minimum cut.
For each cut, define the event that it is the final output. Sum the per-cut lower bounds over these disjoint events and compare with probability one.

State the connected, positive-minimum-cut setting of the contraction argument. If disconnected zero cuts count as vertex partitions, the unrestricted claim fails; an edgeless graph has exponentially many such partitions.
hw2026s1-p3#x: Write an event for outputting each particular minimum cut. Ask whether a single run can output two different cuts.
Use the per-cut contraction survival bound, then sum over the mutually exclusive outputs. Solve the resulting inequality for the number of cuts.
Use fixed-cut success, not success for any cut. Count unordered partitions once and retain the connectedness assumption.
2018A-p1#e: Separate two questions about contraction: does every run terminate quickly, and must every resulting cut be minimum?
Consider a run that contracts an edge of the minimum cut you hoped to preserve. A valid final cut need not be optimal, even though the prescribed contractions finish.
Classify the stated algorithm, not a version with extra verification or indefinite repetition. A valid cut is not necessarily a correct minimum-cut answer.
2025B-p1#c: Treat the grade of a uniformly chosen student as a random variable. Translate ‘fraction of students’ into a probability.

Its expectation is the average grade. For positive average and nonnegative grades, compare the threshold with twice that expectation. Separately inspect the zero-average case if the statement permits it.
Markov requires a positive threshold. If all grades are zero and ‘at least twice the average’ is literal, everyone meets the threshold; mention this boundary case rather than dividing by zero.
2023B-p6#x: Give every element an independent random sign. For one fixed set, express its discrepancy as twice its positive-sign count minus its size.
Apply a two-sided tail bound for that set, using its size or the upper bound from the statement. Make the individual failure probability small enough to sum over all sets.
Did you distinguish the number of sets from the size of each set, keep both tails, and select a constant giving the exact required confidence?
2024A-p2#x: Sample uniformly random assignments, not uniformly random satisfying assignments. Define success by evaluating the entire CNF formula.
Use accuracy one tenth and the exponentially small requested failure probability in the sample bound. This gives a polynomial sample count; each test must scan the formula.
Your runtime must depend on formula size as well as variable count. Returning a count instead of the fraction of successful trials would be the wrong estimator.
2024C-p3#x: Choose a uniformly random binary vector. For one fixed forbidden vector, define indicators for the coordinates where they differ.
The distance is a sum of independent fair indicators with mean half the dimension. Translate distance below one third into a deviation from this mean, then union bound over the supplied set.
Use the problem's bound on the number of forbidden vectors. Prove simultaneous distance from all of them, not merely large expected distance from one.
2025B-p5#x: Sample a uniformly random three-colouring of all vertices, and let success mean every edge is properly coloured.
Substitute error equal to the reciprocal of the vertex count and the stated exponential failure probability. Generate each colouring and scan all edges to test it.
Include vertex generation and edge testing in runtime. This estimates the fraction of legal colourings; it is not an algorithm guaranteed to find one.
2024B-p6#x: Construct the random bipartite graph with the edge probability prescribed by the desired balance. Fix one pair of subsets and count edges between them.

For this pair, independent edge indicators give a concentration bound in the product of the subset sizes. Count possible pairs of subsets of each size before selecting the logarithmic threshold constant.
The union bound is over subset pairs, not just vertices. Check all allowed sizes and the relative-error versus additive-error conversion.
2025A-p4#x: Sample independent uniform sign vectors. Fix one nonempty coordinate subset from the definition of unbiasedness and inspect its parity or sign product on a single sample.
Show that this product has mean zero, then concentrate its empirical average. There are exponentially many coordinate subsets, but only linearly many bits in their count's logarithm.
Check whether the required output is a set or a sample multiset; duplicates require justification. Treat the empty coordinate subset separately, since its product is always one.
hw2026s1-p6#x: For one fixed nonempty test subset, write the sign product for a uniform random sampled vector. Why is it equally likely to be positive and negative?
Convert sign products to fair indicators, concentrate their sample average, and union bound over all test subsets. Solve for a sample count giving failure at most one hundredth.
Verify the precise balance normalization and set-versus-multiset convention. State construction time in terms of vector length and sample count.
hw2025s1-p5#x: Assign independent signs to elements, then focus on a single set's signed sum.
Translate its absolute discrepancy into deviation of a binomial count from its mean. Make the per-set failure small enough for a union bound over the whole family.
Name the random variables, their independence and the number of bad events. Overlap between sets does not invalidate the union bound.
2014A-p8#b: Use the number of unsatisfied clauses as your nonnegative variable. Translate satisfying fewer than three quarters into too many unsatisfied clauses.
Compute the expected unsatisfied count under the random assignment from part (a). Compare it with one quarter of all clauses using Markov.
Do not assume clause-satisfaction events are independent: clauses can share variables. Carefully preserve the strict or non-strict event inclusion.
2015A-p5#x: Write the geometric hit probability for a uniform sample from the specified cube. Express the desired estimate of pi as a constant times the empirical hit fraction.

Convert the required relative accuracy for pi to additive accuracy for that hit probability before applying the concentration inequality. Use a justified bound if the resulting sample count would contain the unknown value.
Check the cube and ball dimensions, the scale factor, the confidence and integer rounding of sample size. Ten percent relative error is not automatically additive error one tenth.
2015B-p5#x: Let the original runtime be the random variable. Propose stopping after a constant multiple of its linear expectation bound.
Choose the timeout so Markov bounds the timeout probability by one tenth. Specify what the bounded-time algorithm outputs if the original has not finished.
Explain why a completed run is correct and only a timeout can cause error. The resulting runtime is worst-case linear, not merely expected linear.
2017A-p4#x: Each uniform random position gives an indicator for observing a one. The sample mean estimates the unknown fraction of ones.
Use additive accuracy one hundredth and failure probability one tenth in the two-sided sample bound. Round up to an integer number of independent samples.
Specify sampling with replacement or justify the alternative concentration theorem. Check that the sample count targets the requested confidence, not its complement.
2018B-p4#e: Distinguish exact randomized selection from a capped attempt that may time out. A completed selection run is correct; the cap introduces the failure event.
Choose the stated cap so one trial times out with probability at most one half. Restart independently, up to five attempts, and multiply the timeout bounds.

If all five time out, the algorithm must report failure, not an unchecked answer. Five capped attempts give a failure-allowing bounded algorithm; indefinite retries of verified attempts give Las Vegas behaviour.
2025A-p1#a: Read ‘at most’ carefully. Let the score be the number of clauses satisfied by a uniform random assignment.
Compute one clause's satisfaction probability under the stated distinct-literal assumptions. After finding the expected score, ask what would happen if every assignment scored strictly above it.
Use averaging in the ‘at most’ direction. Check the clause convention: tautologies or repeated literals can alter the usual three-distinct-variable probability.
2017B-p4#a: Try a uniform random assignment and one indicator per satisfied clause. You only need the weaker threshold requested, not an exact optimum.
Bound the probability that a nonempty clause is satisfied from below by one half. Sum over clauses, then use existence of an outcome at least as good as the average.
Do not claim one assignment satisfies every clause or that clause indicators are independent. State the nonempty-clause assumption.
2023B-p1#d: Check what ‘second eigenvalue’ means in this course: second algebraically largest or second-largest absolute value. Also distinguish being at the target at the final time from visiting it by that time.

Under an absolute-eigenvalue bound, subtract the uniform stationary vector and make its remaining norm smaller than half the reciprocal of the vertex count. If only an algebraic bound is given, a negative eigenvalue near minus one needs separate handling.
State exactly which eigenvalue and event the argument bounds. A mixing-time statement cannot silently ignore periodicity.
2025A-p1#d: Take an eigenvector with eigenvalue one and look at a coordinate where it is maximal.
That coordinate equals the average of neighbouring coordinates. Equality at a maximum forces each neighbour to attain the same maximum; propagate along paths in the connected graph.
Show every coordinate is equal and that the constant vector really is an eigenvector. Connectedness is essential for the one-dimensional conclusion.
2025B-p1#d: Translate singularity of the shifted matrix into an eigenvalue statement for the original matrix. Check connectedness in the question before invoking a bipartiteness characterization.

For a connected regular graph, use an eigenvector of eigenvalue minus one and equality in the neighbour-average bound to force alternating signs on edges. Without connectedness, one bipartite component only establishes the eigenvalue, not that every component is bipartite.
Include the graph's assumptions and normalization. If disconnected graphs are allowed, test a disjoint union of a regular bipartite component and a nonbipartite component of the same degree.
2025C-p3#x: Write the lazy transition matrix as one third identity plus two thirds the original transition matrix. What does this do to each eigenvalue?

Bound the transformed negative eigenvalues away from minus one, and use the connected-graph spectral-gap estimate for the positive side. Choose a polynomial number of steps to make the error from uniform at most half the reciprocal of the vertex count.
Do not assume every lazy eigenvalue is nonnegative with this stay probability. Bound absolute values and distinguish ending at the target from hitting it earlier.
hw2026s2-p1#a: Write the sum of squared coordinates of the normalized eigenvector. For this part, you do not yet need the eigenvalue equation.
Suppose every coordinate magnitude were smaller than the reciprocal square root of the number of coordinates. Sum their squared upper bounds.
The conclusion is about absolute value, not positivity. A sign flip of the whole eigenvector is a separate WLOG step.
hw2026s2-p1#b: Use orthogonality to the constant vector, together with the positive coordinate provided by the preceding part.
If all other coordinates were positive, or even all nonnegative, their sum could not cancel the given positive coordinate. Explain why the relevant eigenvectors are orthogonal.
Justify the eigenvalue separation or connectedness fact needed for orthogonality; then explicitly identify the nonpositive coordinate.
hw2026s2-p1#c: Take a path between the large positive coordinate and the nonpositive coordinate from the previous parts.
The endpoint difference is at least the reciprocal square root of the vertex count. If every edge difference were too small, the sum along a simple path would fall short of that difference.
Use absolute differences and a simple path of bounded length. Do not assume coordinate values change monotonically along the path.
hw2026s2-p1#d: Start by expanding the squared differences in the requested identity. Keep the normalization of the lazy matrix visible.
Replace the quadratic form by the eigenvalue, then retain the edge found in part (c) in the nonnegative sum. Substitute the lazy transition weight and square the coordinate-gap bound.
Track the factor one half, the ordered-pair counting and the degree normalization. A stronger constant is fine only if all counting factors are justified.
hw2026s2-p2#b: Write each coordinate of the two set-indicator vectors and expand the matrix product as a double sum.
Only pairs with first endpoint in the first set and second endpoint in the second set survive. Match each surviving adjacency entry with the ordered edge-count convention.
Use the unnormalized adjacency matrix here. Edges inside the intersection may be counted twice; check that this agrees with the problem's definition.
hw2026s2-p2#c: Subtract each indicator vector's projection onto the constant vector. This separates the expected-density main term from the error term.

The constant component contributes the degree times the product of set sizes divided by the vertex count. Bound the orthogonal bilinear term by the largest absolute nontrivial adjacency eigenvalue times the two vector norms.
Do not mix normalized and unnormalized eigenvalues. Bound the residual norms by the square roots of the set sizes and retain an absolute value around the discrepancy.
hw2025s2-p1#a: Use the unit-length equation for the eigenvector. What is the average of its squared coordinates?
Assume every squared coordinate is smaller than that average and sum over all coordinates to get a contradiction.
State the squared-coordinate conclusion exactly before taking square roots. No independence or probability argument is involved.
hw2025s2-p1#b: Write the inner product with the all-ones vector as a coordinate sum. Recall the positive coordinate chosen in the previous step.
A zero sum with at least one strictly positive term must contain a negative term, hence in particular a nonpositive one.
Explain why the inner product is zero; symmetry and distinct eigenvalues, with the needed connectivity fact, provide this.
hw2025s2-p1#c: Join the positive and nonpositive coordinates by a simple path in the graph.
Telescope the endpoint difference and compare it with the number of edges times the largest edge difference. Insert the lower bound from the preceding parts.
Bound path length by the number of vertices and use absolute values. Cancellation along a path cannot invalidate the triangle-inequality bound.
hw2025s2-p1#d: Identify the stochastic matrix used in this version before substituting any edge weight.
Use the squared-difference identity and keep the large-gap edge from part (c). Its positive transition weight converts the coordinate gap into a lower bound on one minus the eigenvalue.
Check whether the matrix is lazy or not, and use its actual edge weight. Do not import a constant from the other homework version without checking.
hw2025s2-p2#a: Build a vector constant on one connected component and zero elsewhere. What does the normalized adjacency matrix do to it?
Repeat for a second component. These component indicators are independent eigenvectors of eigenvalue one, which is also the largest possible eigenvalue.
Prove multiplicity at least two, not merely the existence of one eigenvector. State the ordering convention for the eigenvalues.
hw2025s2-p2#b: Assign coordinate plus one to one bipartition side and minus one to the other.
Every neighbour has the opposite sign, so the normalized neighbour average negates the coordinate. Then use the spectral range of a symmetric transition matrix.
Show the vector is nonzero and check normalization. Establish that minus one is the smallest eigenvalue, not just an eigenvalue.
2017B-p3#x: Let the cover time be the random variable and relate ‘target not yet visited’ to ‘not all vertices visited’.
Apply the given expectation bound at the stated time horizon. The target's hitting time is bounded by the cover time, so the cover-time tail bound suffices.
Use a subset relation between failure events, not equality. Substitute the exact horizon and take the complement for the requested success probability.
2023A-p1#b: Revisit the isolation proof with all weights except one fixed. Does a product-weight tie still forbid at most one value for the remaining weight?

Separate sets containing the chosen element from those not containing it. Positive fixed weights turn their best products into one quantity linear in the remaining weight and one constant quantity. Count possible bad values and union bound.
Do not quote the sum-version lemma unchanged. Explain positivity, the at-most-one tie value and why multiple minima force a bad element.
2024A-p3#x: For one vertex pair, view simple paths as a family of edge subsets. Positive weights ensure a minimum walk can be taken simple.
Use the number of edges as the ground-set size and union bound the isolation failure over all relevant vertex pairs. Choose a polynomial weight range making the total failure at most one tenth.
Treat pairs with no connecting path according to the question's assumptions. Explain that one shared weight assignment must work simultaneously for all pairs.
2025C-p1#c: There are two uniqueness requirements: a minimum cut and a maximum cut. A single application of minimum-isolation addresses only one.

For maximum weight, apply minimum-isolation to complements of cut edge sets within the full edge set. The total edge weight is common to all cuts. Union bound the two failure events with the given range.
No independence between the two uniqueness events is needed. Check whether cuts are identified by edge sets or vertex partitions, especially for disconnected graphs.
hw2026s2-p3#x: Use Cauchy–Binet to express a determinant whose terms select equally indexed column bases in both matrices.

Assign isolating weights to column indices so a unique minimum-weight common basis gives a unique lowest-degree nonzero term. Use the symbolic determinant for detection, then explain how to recover actual columns if required.
Show what happens when there is no common basis, why the isolated coefficient cannot cancel, and why polynomial weights keep the algebraic representation manageable.
hw2025s2-p3#x: Introduce a variable tracking the number of red edges in a matching. The coefficient at the requested red count is the quantity to inspect.

Use isolation within the family of matchings having exactly the required red count. Explain how the prescribed powers of two distinguish the isolated minimum term despite determinant signs, and how matching edges are recovered.
Track bit lengths as well as arithmetic operations. If extracting a matching, justify each self-reduction query and account for all failure probabilities.
